title: Haumai: the disease with its own cure
hook: ego is a chronic illness, says a salok of Guru Angad, and the cure lies within it too (Asa di Var, ang 466)

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukam, the order in everything; your line was in tune. Yesterday ended with I, I, I. Today, that I.

When someone is bitten by a venomous snake, the treatment, antivenom, is made using the venom itself. A tiny, careful dose of the poison is used to teach an animal's body to fight it, and from that comes the cure. The thing that harms you becomes the way you're healed. It sounds like a riddle, but it saves lives. Guru Angad, the second Guru, wrote a short verse that works like that riddle. It names an illness, a lasting one, and then says where the medicine is hidden.
screen: `A SNAKEBITE.` → `THE CURE MADE FROM THE VENOM.` → `A RIDDLE THAT HEALS.`

segments.voice: Today's word is haumai. Say it: HAU-mai. Hau means I. Mai means me. Haumai: I-me, the self that puts itself at the center of everything. English usually says ego, but haumai is more everyday than that sounds: the voice that says my turn, my way, my hurt, my credit, all day long. You met it in the Japji: whoever understands the hukam stops saying I, I, I. Now open the Granth to ang 466, to a long hymn called Asa di Var, the ballad sung in the early morning. There, a salok of Guru Angad describes haumai like a doctor. This is its nature, he says: in haumai people act, in haumai they're bound, and they keep coming back to be born again. Then the diagnosis, in his own words: haumai deeragh rog hai. Haumai is a chronic disease. Deeragh means long, lasting; not a cold you get over in a week. And then the riddle: daaroo bhee is maahi. The medicine is in it too. Commentators read this in more than one way. Some hear that the very self that says I can turn around and say Waheguru, the same energy pointed toward the One. Others hear that the cure is found inside the person, not outside. The salok goes on: if the One shows grace, a person lives by the Guru's word, and in that discipline the pain goes. So the illness is inside, and so is the cure. You don't have to travel anywhere to find it.
screen: `HAUMAI — I-ME.` · `A CHRONIC DISEASE, SAYS GURU ANGAD.` · `DAAROO BHEE IS MAAHI.` · `THE SAME SELF, TURNED AROUND.` · then, large: `THE CURE IS INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last day and find one me-first moment: an interruption, a need to be right, a hurt that nobody noticed you. Don't scold yourself; just see it clearly, like a doctor noticing a symptom. Then picture the same moment with the same energy turned outward, the interruption becoming listening, the need to be right becoming curiosity, and breathe with that until it settles.
Haumai. I-me: the self that puts itself at the center. Guru Angad calls it a chronic disease, and says the medicine is in it too.
Your line: the cure is inside. Haumai, the long illness, carries its own medicine. Two hundred thirty-six days in.

howItsDone: Asa di Var, which holds this salok, is sung in many gurdwaras in the early morning; Sikh teachers often describe haumai as the root illness that remembering the Name and living by the Guru's word are meant to heal.

trapdoor: what you thought: ego means being arrogant.
what it means: haumai is the everyday I-me at the center of everything, a chronic illness with its own medicine.
what a scholar hears: hau and mai are both first-person words; deeragh is Sanskrit dirgha, long; the salok is Mahala 2 in Asa di Var.
recall: the Guru's Word, for Sikhs the Guru itself
